analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices and offers seniors a government-run prescription drug plan option.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, sitting there until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change Medicare's prescription drug program in several ways: it would let the Health and Human Services Secretary negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers (something a 2003 law currently forbids), create a government-run drug plan available nationwide with a $35 monthly premium for 2008, guarantee every senior at least three plan choices including that public option, fully reimburse employers who keep covering retirees' drugs, and restore coverage for benzodiazepines, a class of anxiety and sleep medications Medicare was barred from covering. It would also repeal several subsidy and stabilization programs that benefit private Medicare Advantage insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 40 million seniors and disabled Americans, would gain access to lower drug prices through government negotiation and a low-premium public plan option they could pick over private plans. Employers who provide retiree drug coverage would be fully repaid for it. People who take benzodiazepines would get coverage for medications currently excluded.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' clause that bars the HHS Secretary from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers, and directs the Secretary to negotiate contracts so beneficiaries 'pay the lowest possible price' [S2][S3].
Creates a nationwide government-run prescription drug plan with a $35 monthly premium in 2008, offered in addition to — not instead of — private plans, giving seniors a public option [S2][S3].
Guarantees every Part D beneficiary a choice of at least three plans in their area, including the public plan, and requires that no single company be the only plan sponsor available [S3].
Provides full reimbursement to employers for the cost of qualified retiree drug coverage, aiming to keep employers from dropping retiree benefits [S2][S3].

Removes the statutory exclusion of benzodiazepines from Medicare drug coverage, restoring access to a class of medications used for anxiety, sleep disorders, and seizures, while directing HHS to set prescribing safeguards against overuse and abuse [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear lower prices from government negotiation. Private prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers would face new competition from a government-run plan at a $35 premium, likely forcing them to cut premiums or exit. Taxpayers could bear the cost if the government plan's $35 premium is set below its true cost, and repealing the insurers' stabilization fund removes a government backstop for private regional plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

drawbacks.text: The bill forbids the Secretary from imposing a national formulary or price structure, so the negotiation power would be limited compared with programs like the VA, which can simply refuse to cover drugs that cost too much [S3].
The government plan's $35 premium is set by statute rather than actuarial cost; if actual drug costs run higher, taxpayers would make up the difference [S3].

Repealing the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund and the comparative cost adjustment program removes protections meant to keep private plans in rural and underserved markets, which could reduce plan choices in some areas [S2][S3].
Restoring benzodiazepine coverage raises the risk of long-term overuse and abuse, which the bill attempts to manage only through a review of plan policies and physician education guidelines [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gains — negotiated drug prices and a cheap public plan option — would go directly to seniors and would likely pressure private plans to lower premiums. The counterweights are real but modest: the negotiation power is softer than what other federal buyers already use, the public plan's premium could shift costs to taxpayers, and repealing insurer stabilization programs could thin out plan choices in some markets. On balance the bill transfers bargaining power from drug makers and insurers to beneficiaries, and its most questionable feature is the politically fixed $35 premium.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on the Senate's first day of the 2007 session and referred to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it; it stayed there until the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Cardin introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, the first day of the 110th Congress [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever taken [S5].
No senators signed on as cosponsors over the full two-year Congress [S4].
The Finance Committee held no markup or vote, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers kept the 2003 law's ban on Medicare price negotiation, and private Part D insurers kept their market free of a government-run competitor. Seniors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the 110th Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in the committee for the full two-year Congress.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote during the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no roll-call votes were ever taken, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 'non-interference' clause that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices, exposing manufacturers to the bulk-buying leverage other federal agencies use. Lower negotiated prices would show up as lower costs for beneficiaries and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Private prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: A nationwide government-run plan at a $35 premium would compete directly with private plans, and the bill repeals the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund that backstops private regional plans. Private plans would keep their role but only by winning against a public competitor.

The bill requires full reimbursement of employer spending on qualified retiree drug coverage, reducing the incentive to drop retiree benefits. Retirees are the intended beneficiary of that protection.
